Why Finca Mirjam stands out

Finca Mirjam sits in the lush hills of Dipilto — an area celebrated for its biodiversity and vibrant birdlife. Volcanic soil, gentle slopes, and a misty microclimate create ideal conditions for producing clean, sweet, and balanced coffees, with excellent sunlight and natural airflow supporting even drying.

Led by Martha Lucía Albir Sotomayor, a third-generation coffee producer and advocate for women in coffee, Finca Mirjam combines heritage with innovation. The name itself is a tribute — honouring the family legacy that has shaped this land for generations and a shared commitment to the future of sustainable specialty coffee.

Recognized multiple times in Nicaragua's Cup of Excellence, Finca Mirjam continues to build its reputation as one of the most promising farms in the region. In 2025, the team is piloting selective fermentation protocols that will shape a dedicated micro-lot program beginning with the 2026 harvest.

Processing in detail — washed lots
1

Selective hand-picking

Only fully ripe cherries are harvested. Unripe, dry, and overripe fruit is removed during field-level sorting to ensure lot uniformity.

2

Floating and resting

Sorted cherries are floated in clean water to eliminate impurities. They then rest piled for 24 hours before pulping.

3

Pulping and tank fermentation

Cherries are pulped ~24 hours after harvest, then fermented for 24–36 hours in clean tanks. No additives.

4

Washing and transport to dry mill

After fermentation, parchment is thoroughly washed with clean water and transported to Cafetos de Segovia's dry mill.

5

Controlled drying (~12 days)

Days 1–3 (from ~56% humidity): full sun on African raised beds or patios. Days 4–11 (from ~42%): moved to shaded drying for even airflow, preventing over-fermentation or mold. Day 12: brief sun finish to reach target humidity of 12%. Humidity is continuously monitored by Cafetos de Segovia.

About the region — Nueva Segovia, Nicaragua

Nueva Segovia occupies Nicaragua's northern highlands, pressed against the Honduran border at elevations that regularly exceed 1,200 metres. The combination of crisp nights, morning mist rolling through the valleys, and volcanic soils creates the kind of slow cherry maturation that specialty coffee demands — complexity built unhurriedly, over weeks on the tree.

The Dipilto area within Nueva Segovia is particularly special. Dense forest cover, rich biodiversity, and some of the highest bird populations in the country signal an ecosystem in balance — the same conditions that give farms like Mirjam their distinctive cup character: clean, sweet, and layered with floral and citrus notes.

Nicaragua's Maracaturra — a cross between the large-beaned Maragogype and the compact Caturra — thrives here. Its expressive complexity and large bean size have made it the flagship variety of the region, consistently recognised at the Nicaragua Cup of Excellence.
